title: How To Manage Classroom Behavior During Assemblies https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2011/01/15/classroom-management-during-assemblies/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a three-step system for managing student behavior during school assemblies, an environment many teachers dread because of reduced control. The first step is modeling exactly how students should sit, be attentive, clap, and behave, done in exaggerated detail on the classroom carpet before the assembly. The second is modeling the opposite - deliberately acting out unwanted behaviors so students recognize and laugh at them, reinforcing the lesson. The third is bringing the classroom management plan physically into the assembly via a clipboard, using it to quietly note rule violations and hand signals (for warnings and time-outs) rather than confronting students in the moment, with consequences enforced later back in the classroom. The result, he argues, is a calmer assembly experience for the teacher and clearer, less stressful accountability for students.
points: Detailed, even exaggerated modeling of both correct and incorrect assembly behavior cements expectations before the event.
A "how-not-to" demonstration lets students recognize and laugh at unwanted behaviors, reinforcing the lesson.
Bringing the classroom management plan into the assembly via a clipboard extends accountability beyond the classroom.
Quiet hand signals for warnings and time-outs let the teacher note violations without confronting students mid-assembly.
Consequences are enforced back in the classroom rather than on the spot, avoiding a public disruption.
quotes: Managing behavior during school assemblies can be a challenge. But it doesn’t have to be.
Keep it simple, but make your modeling highly detailed, even exaggerated. This is key to its effectiveness.
The more over-the-top the modeling is, the more effective it will be.
When students are able to experience, in a highly detailed way, the absurdity and rudeness of their behavior, the lesson will hit home.
Your classroom management plan should follow you wherever you go, including school assemblies. Take a clipboard with you to the assembly and take note of any behavior that breaks your class rules.
If you’ve faithfully followed steps one and two, you’ll notice your students looking up at you often during the assembly–checking in to see how they’re doing.
You can breathe easy in knowing that the clipboard you’re carrying does your speaking for you.
